name: Glacier National Park
tagline: Glacier-carved peaks, emerald lakes and the Going-to-the-Sun Road.

photo.alt: A small historic building strapped to a mountain top with other snowy peaks in the background
photo.caption: Swiftcurrent Fire Lookout

intro: The historic Going-to-the-Sun Road, built in the late 1920s and early 1930s, stretches over 50 miles through glacier-carved peaks, emerald-blue alpine lakes and lush forests. The park had over 100 glaciers in 1910; by 2015 only 26 still met the size criteria for active glaciers, and many families come hoping to see one. Here a final adventure can be a boardwalk among ancient cedars, a lake below waterfalls or a long climb to the ice itself.
scatterSummary: Scattering requires a special use permit and is allowed only in undeveloped areas, at least 200 feet from any developed location such as a road, trail or lake.
scatterFacts: Complete the Application for Special Use Permit, Spreading of Ashes, and email it to glac_sup@nps.gov. Park phone: 406-888-7800.

The park replies with a letter that is your permit; its instructions on location and notification are the permit's terms. At least one member of the party must carry the letter or a copy while scattering.
Only in undeveloped areas: not within 200 feet of any developed location, such as a road, trail, building, parking lot, boat ramp, swimming beach, campground or lake.
Ashes must be scattered, not left in any container. No marker or memorial of any sort may be placed.
The park does not list a fee for this permit. Its general rule is that special use permit applications must arrive at least 20 business days before the requested date.
Winter-like weather can occur at any time of year, usually November through April, and may make an area impossible to reach.

scatterLink.label: Permits and reservations: spreading of ashes (NPS)

beforeYouGo: Vehicle reservations are not required anywhere in the park in 2026. Portions of Going-to-the-Sun Road stay open all year, but a drive across the whole road is possible only in summer. From July 1 to September 7, 2026, private vehicle parking at Logan Pass is limited to three hours (free timestamped permit from the kiosk), and the park is piloting a ticketed-only Logan Pass shuttle. Many Glacier is reached by turning off Highway 89 on the east side of the park.

destinations.name: Trail of the Cedars
destinations.description: Under the old-growth cedars beside Avalanche Creek, the forest feels hushed and green. The boardwalk loop carries you through the grove to where the water has carved Avalanche Gorge, a narrow channel of rushing blue and white. Listen for the American dippers bobbing along the creek. Everyone can come, wheelchairs included, which makes this a place to walk side by side at an easy pace and share the memories that matter most.

plan.distance: 0.9 mi loop (the park's accessibility page lists 0.7 mi of accessible trail)
plan.accessibility: Wheelchair accessible: wood boardwalk and polymer pavement (NPS)
plan.scattering: With a permit, in undeveloped areas away from this spot

drive.route: Going-to-the-Sun Road about 16 miles from the West Entrance to the Avalanche Picnic Area, also served by the park shuttle.

trail.name: Trail of the Cedars
steps: Start at the Avalanche Picnic Area.
Follow the boardwalk loop through the cedars to the view of Avalanche Gorge, then back to the start.

scatterNote.text: Scattering is not allowed within 200 feet of trails, roads, picnic areas or lakes. With a permit, the park's letter gives instructions on location; describe an undeveloped area that meets the rules in your application.

destinations.name: Avalanche Lake

photo.alt: A first dusting of snow decorates the rocky peaks above the fall colors of the mountain lake basin

destinations.description: Beyond the cedars, the trail climbs steadily through old-growth forest until the trees part at an alpine lake with waterfalls spilling down the mountainsides above it. The park calls it an excellent introduction to what Glacier is all about. Find a spot along the shore where everyone can sit, unpack lunch and watch the falls together, and give the afternoon to stories about the one who would have loved this walk.

plan.distance: 2.3 mi one way (about 5 mi round trip)
plan.difficulty: Not rated by NPS; the park says the trail becomes steeper, rocky and more challenging beyond the first half mile
plan.accessibility: The first half mile is the accessible Trail of the Cedars; beyond it the trail becomes steeper, rocky and more challenging (NPS)
plan.scattering: With a permit, in undeveloped areas away from this spot

drive.route: Going-to-the-Sun Road about 16 miles from the West Entrance to the Avalanche Picnic Area, also served by the park shuttle.

trail.name: Trail of the Cedars, then the Avalanche Lake Trail
steps: Follow the Trail of the Cedars from the Avalanche Picnic Area to the Avalanche Lake Trailhead.
Climb steadily through old-growth forest to the foot of the lake.
notes: Pets are not allowed. NPS sources differ on the elevation gain.

scatterNote.text: Scattering is not allowed within 200 feet of trails or lakes. With a permit, the park's letter gives instructions on location; describe an undeveloped area that meets the rules in your application.

destinations.name: Hidden Lake Overlook
destinations.description: From Logan Pass, at the top of Going-to-the-Sun Road, a boardwalk and trail climb through alpine meadows cradled by Clements and Reynolds Mountains, where wildflowers and wildlife are often close at hand. At the overlook, Hidden Lake lies far below, and with binoculars you can pick out the headwall of Sperry Glacier beyond it. Stand together in this high, open place and let it hold your goodbye for a while.

plan.difficulty: Not rated by NPS; the park calls it a less challenging hike, mostly on a boardwalk with stairs
plan.accessibility: Wooden boardwalk and packed soil, with several sets of stairs and switchbacks; NPS calls it a less challenging hike
plan.bestTime: Summer, when the whole of Going-to-the-Sun Road is open
plan.scattering: With a permit, in undeveloped areas away from this spot

drive.route: Going-to-the-Sun Road to Logan Pass. From July 1 to September 7, 2026, parking there is limited to three hours; a ticketed shuttle also runs.

trail.name: Hidden Lake Trail
steps: Start at the Hidden Lake Trailhead behind the Logan Pass Visitor Center.
Follow the boardwalk and trail, with stairs and switchbacks, to the Hidden Lake Overlook.
Many visitors turn back here; the trail continues to Hidden Lake itself.
notes: Snow can cover the boardwalk early in the season. The Going-to-the-Sun Road page lists 1.4 mi and 460 ft from the visitor center.

scatterNote.text: Scattering is not allowed within 200 feet of trails, buildings, parking lots or lakes. With a permit, the park's letter gives instructions on location; describe an undeveloped area that meets the rules in your application.

destinations.name: Grinnell Glacier

photo.alt: Mountain ridge with glacier snow and ice above teal lake

destinations.description: Grinnell Glacier asks for a long day, and gives back one of the most remarkable sights in the park. The mostly open trail climbs past wildflowers and mountain views until the glacier and the lake at its foot come into view. The glacier lost 45 percent of its area between 1966 and 2015, and standing before it carries a quiet sense of time passing. For the strong hikers in your family, reaching it together is a tribute to a life well lived.

plan.distance: 5.0 mi one way from the trailhead; 3.7 mi one way from the concessioner boat drop-off
plan.difficulty: Not rated by NPS; the park calls it a very challenging day hike
plan.elevation: 2,596 ft from the trailhead; 2,461 ft from the boat
plan.accessibility: Long, mostly exposed mountain trail; NPS calls it a very challenging day hike
plan.scattering: With a permit, in undeveloped areas away from this spot

drive.route: Highway 89 on the east side of the park, then about 11 miles on Many Glacier Road to the Many Glacier Hotel. The trailhead is at the south end of the hotel parking lot.

trail.name: Grinnell Glacier Trail
steps: Walk from the trailhead, or reserve concessioner boat tickets to be dropped off 1.3 miles closer.
Climb the mostly exposed trail to the Grinnell Glacier Viewpoint above Upper Grinnell Lake.
notes: Another NPS page lists 5.3 mi and 1,600 ft of gain to the viewpoint. Bring plenty of food and water; mountain weather changes quickly.

scatterNote.text: Scattering is not allowed within 200 feet of trails or lakes. With a permit, the park's letter gives instructions on location; describe an undeveloped area that meets the rules in your application.
